cards.title: Steve Beckhardt
cards.sub: c. 1985 · Iris Associates, the fourth engineer
cards.prompt: Ozzie had written the document store and Halvorsen the index on top of it. Name the thing they found they had underestimated, and say why it is a separate problem from the store rather than a feature of it.
cards.answer: Synchronisation and replication — Ozzie says they saw it about six months in and hired someone for it. A store answers 'what is here now'. Replication has to answer 'what happened elsewhere while we were apart', which needs per-document edit history, a rule for picking a survivor, and a policy for divergence. None of that is anything the store has a reason to carry.
cards.body: Fourth engineer at Iris Associates. Ray Ozzie had written the document store, Tim Halvorsen the indexing layer, Len Kawell the interface; Beckhardt got replication. Ozzie's oral history names him twice — once as the hire made when distribution stopped being a feature of the database, once in the list of people without whom there would be no Lotus Notes.

cards.title: Replication or Save Conflict
cards.sub: HCL Domino 10.0.1 help · the same string is in the Domino 12 docs
cards.prompt: Notes has two kinds of conflict: a save conflict and a replication conflict. One is settled at the instant of saving, the other only afterwards. Which is which, and what fact about the two writers decides that?
cards.answer: A save conflict happens inside one replica, so the server can already see the other edit: the first save becomes the main document and the second writer is prompted on the spot. A replication conflict happens across replicas that were apart, so neither writer could see the other; the survivor is chosen after the fact from $Revisions — most saves wins, ties go to the most recent save. The dividing line is whether the two writers were ever visible to each other at save time.
cards.body: Two edits to one document between replications. Domino reads the $Revisions field — 'the date and time of each document editing session' — names one copy the main document and keeps the other, unaltered, as a response document titled Replication or Save Conflict. No merge, no overwrite. ACL and design changes are exempt.

cards.title: Oral History of Raymond (Ray) Ozzie
cards.sub: Computer History Museum · CHM Reference X9392.2021
cards.prompt: 'Lotus Notes shipped on 7 December 1989' gets repeated as a hard fact. Say what kind of source that date actually rests on here, and restate the date in the strongest form that source honestly supports.
cards.answer: It rests on an oral history — Ozzie interviewed by Marc Weber for the Computer History Museum on 10 December 2020, so a recollection thirty-one years after the event, not a shipping record. What he says is 'our first sale was on December 7th of ’89'. The honest form is therefore: Ozzie recalled that the first sale was 7 December 1989 — a sale, recalled, not a ship date documented.
cards.body: Interviewed by Marc Weber, recorded over Zoom on 10 December 2020, 54 pages, free PDF from the CHM archive. It also carries Lotus's $1.2 million cheque with no equity attached, the dial-up store-and-forward model the replication engine was built on, and the point at which replication got an engineer of its own.

cards.title: Where the loser gets filed
cards.prompt: Notes files the losing edit as a response document under the winner. Dropbox keeps it as a peer in the same folder, with the editor's name and the save date written into the filename. Both preserve everything, so name what the second arrangement buys — and the thing neither of them fixes.
cards.answer: It buys discovery. A sibling whose name says who made it and when is found by the person who can merge it, with no need to know the system has a hierarchy worth looking under; a child record has to be gone looking for. What neither fixes: preserving both copies only relocates the decision onto a human. Domino's merge option runs only 'if no fields conflict', so two people editing the same field still end up with two objects and a person who has to reconcile them.
cards.body: Dropbox: 'The editor's username, conflicted copy, and the save date will be added to the filename.' Same policy as Domino's — detect, refuse to merge, keep both — moved up one level, out of a child record and into the user's own namespace, where the filename does the explaining.
